So when you download a font to use, for example, whether it's a local font like this, or you're downloading a font, for example, from Google Fonts over here, you're going to need some time for that font to be fetched from your server and downloaded. But meanwhile, the user is actually looking at your page before this may be downloaded. They may be waiting for it to download.

But the text is still on their screen. So there's different phases that your font goes through. There's the block phase, where at this phase there is no text that shows up. It just renders invisible text on your page. The next phase is what's called the swap phase, and the swap phase says, okay, your text hasn't loaded yet. We don't have the font yet. So we're going to render a fallback font. In our case, this SansSeraph font. But as soon as our font does load, it's going to full go back to our normal font instead of using the fallback.

And then there's a failure state. And that essentially says, we waited too long, we could not actually get to your font. So we're just going to permanently load this Sans serif fallback instead of loading the font that you actually wanted, because we assume that it failed. So by setting our font display to block, what happens is the amount of time that our text waits while it's invisible before it displays the fallback is going to be a very long period of time, much longer than normal. While if we set our font display to swap,

Our actual blocking portion where the font is invisible is going to be very short, but the amount of time where we show the fallback and wait before actually declaring a failure is going to be long. So essentially we'll display this fallback sooner and we'll still display our normal font as soon as it loads, but our failure state is going to be pushed off later. The next type of property here is called fallback. And what this fallback essentially is saying, we want to have another very short period of time where we block.

So it's going to be very short, just like with swap. But this says that our swap duration is going to be shorter. So essentially, we're only waiting a couple seconds where we show this fallback font. **Something that used to be incredibly difficult to do in CSS was animating between a height of zero or any other value to a height of auto. This is currently impossible to do with the code that we have written right now. If I try to do a transition on my height property, we'll do a nice and slow two-second animation when I click**

**You notice it just instantly appears and disappears. But if we want to be able to animate this property smoothly, what we need to do is to use a property called interpolate size. This is a very interesting property that has two values. We have numeric only. This is the default behavior where you can only do animations between numeric values, like 10 pixels, 20 pixels. Or we can say allow keywords.**

**And what this is going to do is allow us to do animations between something like a height of auto to a value like a height of zero. Now when I click, you notice it actually properly does this animation. It was just one single line of CSS to completely fix this animation. So if you're ever trying to figure out why your animations between height zero and height auto no longer work, it's because you need to enable this interpolate size property. Now this is currently a very experimental property. You can see I don't get any support inside of VS Code, it has no idea what this even is.**

**And it's currently only available in the Chrome browser. So this is quite an experimental feature. But hopefully, in the future, when you're watching this video, it'll be something that will eventually make it to all websites so you can start using it. And the really nice thing about this is even if it doesn't work, for example, you're in Firefox and this is broken, you still can get the behavior to work, you just don't get the really nice and smooth animation.
